title: API 510 Training in Seattle: Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced online API 510 exam prep for Puget Sound vessel inspectors: coke drums, FCC and hydrotreater vessels, Washington boiler rules and instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Seattle: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Cherry Point, Ferndale, Anacortes and Tacoma
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors around Puget Sound

Seattle has no refinery inside its city limits, yet it sits halfway along Washington's refining shoreline. Five refineries stand on Puget Sound and the Strait of Georgia, from Blaine near the Canadian border to the Tacoma tideflats, and their columns, reactors, drums and exchanger shells keep a steady population of vessel inspectors at work. This page is for those inspectors, for the NDT technicians who take the readings, and for engineers who want API 510 behind their name on a vessel report.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Seattle. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers questions as you work through the codes, so a candidate in Ballard, Everett, Mount Vernon or Bellingham can study around whatever rota the plant runs. The American Petroleum Institute decides eligibility, administers the API 510 examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. The course prepares you for that examination; it does not certify you, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Five refineries, read as families of vessels

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey, reporting the position at the start of 2026, lists five operating refineries in Washington with 648,200 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation capacity between them. The table shows each plant's crude capacity and, in barrels per stream day, the conversion units where most of its heavy-walled vessels sit.

Some EIA names differ from the ones used on site. EIA files bp's plant under BP Products North America at Ferndale; bp calls it the Cherry Point refinery, and the Washington Department of Ecology gives its address as Blaine and dates it to 1971. The Anacortes plant EIA lists as Tesoro Refining & Marketing is owned by Marathon Petroleum, which Ecology says does business there as Tesoro, and EIA's Tacoma entry, U.S. Oil & Refining, is owned by Par Pacific.

Read each column as a set of inspection problems. Coking capacity means coke drums cycling between hot fill and water quench. Catalytic cracking means a reactor, regenerator, cyclones and main fractionator in hot, erosive duty, much of it refractory-lined. The Cherry Point hydrocracker and the hydrotreaters behind every plant's desulfurization capacity mean thick, often clad reactors and high-pressure separators in hydrogen. EIA also lists solvent deasphalting at the Marathon plant, asphalt production at Tacoma and sulfur recovery at all five, so the vessel mix runs from heavy-oil extraction columns to sulfur condensers.

How Washington's boiler law treats a refinery vessel

Washington regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels under chapter 70.79 RCW, administered by the Department of Labor and Industries (L&I), with the detail in chapter 296-104 WAC. Three provisions shape a vessel inspector's work on the Sound.

  • Which code governs. WAC 296-104-102 makes Part 2 of the National Board Inspection Code the in-service standard for nonnuclear boilers and unfired pressure vessels, then lets an owner/user inspection agency in petroleum or chemical processing choose the current edition of API 510 for its vessels instead. That clause is how API 510 enters Washington law.
  • How often. WAC 296-104-100 sets biennial external inspections for unfired pressure vessels, and biennial internals where a vessel is subject to corrosion and its construction permits one. Vessels in an owner-user inspection programme may follow NBIC or API 510 intervals instead, and a vessel not subject to corrosion needs no internal inspection.
  • Who qualifies as an owner/user agency. WAC 296-104-010 defines one as an owner or user that maintains an established inspection department whose organisation and procedures meet a nationally recognised standard acceptable to L&I.

RCW 70.79.080 leaves some equipment out, including unfired vessels designed for no more than 15 psig, vessels of five cubic feet or less outside places of public assembly, vessels under federal regulation and ambient-temperature water tanks with no air cushion. Most refinery process vessels stay in scope, so a Washington API 510 inspector works to two calendars: the code's remaining-life logic and the state's certificate cycle, closed when L&I's chief boiler inspector issues a certificate of inspection.

Pressure vessels beyond the refinery fence

Refineries employ most of the region's API 510 inspectors, but pulp and paper has vessels too. Port Townsend Paper, on the Olympic Peninsula, runs a kraft pulp and paper mill that Ecology says makes about 1,000 tons of paper, containerboard and unbleached pulp a day. Washington's rules carry two mill-specific provisions: paper machine dryer rolls may go to five-year inspections under TAPPI TIP 0402-16 when the owner has a written programme the inspector accepts, and black liquor recovery boilers are excluded from the longer internal interval the state allows power boilers in owner-user programmes. The list has also shrunk: WestRock closed its Tacoma linerboard, kraft paper and pulp mill in 2023.

Puget Sound Energy's liquefied natural gas facility on Port of Tacoma property, commissioned in 2022, fuels TOTE Maritime Alaska ships and holds gas in reserve for the coldest days. Large refrigerated LNG tanks are generally designed to low-pressure tank standards such as API 620 and API 625 rather than to Section VIII, so the tank itself usually sits outside API 510, while the exchangers, separators and receivers of a liquefaction plant are vessel work.

Damage mechanisms that decide a Puget Sound vessel plan

The API 510 Body of Knowledge takes its damage material from API RP 571, and the five Washington refineries cover a good share of that catalogue. Learn each mechanism against a vessel you can picture.

  • Hydrogen at temperature. Hydrocracker and hydrotreater reactors and their hot separators are where high temperature hydrogen attack is assessed against API RP 941, and where overlay disbonding and temper embrittlement of older chromium-molybdenum steels come up at shutdown.
  • Wet hydrogen sulfide. Sour water strippers, amine regenerators and their reflux drums, and the FCC gas plant collect blistering, hydrogen-induced cracking and stress-oriented HIC, usually looked for with wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing of internal welds when the vessel is open.
  • Coke drum cycling. Repeated heating and quenching works on the skirt-to-shell junction and the circumferential seams, so drum inspection leans on crack detection and on tracking shell distortion rather than on wall loss alone.
  • The marine air outside. Damp, salty air works on saddles, nozzle necks and insulation of vessels near the water, and insulated austenitic stainless steel can crack externally from chlorides.
  • Cold test water. Winter hydrotests on older carbon steel vessels with no impact test record make the code's advice on metal temperature during the test, relative to the minimum design metal temperature, a practical matter.

Worked example: can an on-stream inspection replace the internal?

An owner-user programme that follows API 510 works to the code's intervals, and API 510 lets the inspector substitute an on-stream inspection for an internal one under stated conditions. The 2006 edition listed them as below; check the wording and clause number in the edition on your effectivity sheet. Where entry is physically possible, all must hold:

  1. the general corrosion rate is known to be less than 0.005 in. (0.125 mm) per year;
  2. the remaining life is greater than 10 years;
  3. the corrosive character of the contents, including trace components, has been established by at least five years in the same or similar service;
  4. the external inspection found no questionable condition;
  5. the shell runs below the creep-rupture range of its material;
  6. the vessel is not subject to environmental cracking or hydrogen damage from its fluid;
  7. there is no non-integrally bonded liner such as strip or plate lining.

Three hypothetical vessels at a north Sound refinery, each with its required thickness given:

  • Diesel product coalescer. 0.577 in. twelve years ago, 0.541 in. today, required 0.402 in. Rate = 0.036 ÷ 12 = 0.003 in. per year; remaining life = 0.139 ÷ 0.003 = about 46 years. Same service since start-up, clean external, ambient temperature, no cracking mechanism, no liner: it qualifies, at the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years, so 10 years unless an RBI assessment justifies otherwise.
  • Crude overhead accumulator. 0.488 in. eight years ago, 0.440 in. today, required 0.330 in. Rate = 0.048 ÷ 8 = 0.006 in. per year; remaining life = 0.110 ÷ 0.006 = about 18 years. The life passes but the rate fails, so the next inspection is internal, at no more than about nine years.
  • Amine regenerator reflux drum. 0.512 in. ten years ago, 0.494 in. today, required 0.310 in. A rate of 0.0018 in. per year leaves about 100 years, yet wet hydrogen sulfide makes the drum susceptible to environmental cracking, so condition six fails and no wall thickness rescues it.

Exam questions of this kind hide the failing condition in the service description rather than the arithmetic. The code also allows an RBI assessment that finds the risk acceptably low, with external NDE effective for the expected damage, to support an on-stream inspection where the list fails.

Routes into API 510 for Puget Sound workers

API 510 eligibility combines education with experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency: one year of inspection with a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, and two, three or five-plus years with a two-year degree, a high school diploma or no formal education, each of those including at least a year of inspection. See API 510 certification requirements for the full rules.

The agency definition matters here because the large refineries run their own inspection departments. API 510 counts the inspection organisation of an owner or user that inspects only its own equipment, and an independent organisation or individual under contract to and under the direction of the owner/user. API reviews the experience you describe; the course does not count toward it.

  • Process operators. Bellingham Technical College's Process Technology associate degree names the four refineries in Whatcom and Skagit counties as its main Washington employers. Whether that degree counts as a two-year engineering or technology credential is API's decision.
  • NDT technicians. Thickness surveys and wet fluorescent magnetic particle work build code familiarity, but API wants inspection experience: planning, evaluating and recording. Earlier-career technicians can see NDT training in Seattle.
  • Welders and repair supervisors. Repair and alteration work counts toward the construction and repair side, and many welding inspectors hold a CWI before API 510; see AWS CWI exam prep in Seattle.

Studying for API 510 from Seattle

Marathon places its Anacortes refinery about 70 miles north of Seattle, and Ferndale and Cherry Point lie further north again, so Seattle-based inspectors often spend part of the week near site. A self-paced course travels with you: a lesson in the evening, practice questions on a quiet night shift, a message to the instructor when a clause will not make sense. Plan around the outage calendar:

  • Before the outage: closed-book foundations, from intervals and corrosion-rate rules to pressure testing, rerating and the RP 571 mechanisms on your sheet.
  • During it: little formal study, but every opened vessel is a lesson in internals, overlay and the methods chosen.
  • After it: the open-book half, with Section VIII Division 1 formulas, the UW-12 joint efficiency table and Section IX variables practised in a PDF until navigation is quick.

Prometric lists test centres in and around Seattle. Each exam window has its own application deadline, so book once API accepts you, and allow north Sound candidates a full day for the drive and the examination.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Puget Sound site

Refinery inspection departments, contractors who staff north Sound turnarounds and mills with their own vessel inspectors can enrol several candidates together, some preparing for API 570 or API 653 at the same time. Fees are quoted on request. Every candidate files a separate API application and works through the material at their own pace, sending questions to the instructor. Owners who need NDE and data review on Washington vessels can see API 510 vessel inspection support in Washington.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in Seattle?
faq.a: No. Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad, and the API 510 course has no in-person sessions in Washington or anywhere else. It is self-paced and online, with an instructor answering your questions as you study, so you can prepare from home, from a motel near Anacortes or between shifts at Cherry Point. Once API accepts your application, you sit the examination at a Prometric test centre in the window you booked.

faq.q: Does Washington L&I accept API 510 for refinery pressure vessels?
faq.a: Yes, as an option for owner/user inspection agencies. WAC 296-104-102 names Part 2 of the National Board Inspection Code as the in-service standard but lets an owner/user inspection agency in petroleum or chemical processing choose the current edition of API 510 for its pressure vessels. WAC 296-104-100 then lets vessels in an owner-user inspection programme follow API 510 intervals in place of the state's biennial default. L&I's chief boiler inspector still issues the certificate of inspection.

faq.q: Does experience on pulp mill vessels count toward API 510?
faq.a: It may. API asks for experience in the activities API 510 describes, gained with an authorized inspection agency, and the code is written around refining and chemical process vessels. A mill inspector who plans vessel inspections, evaluates thickness data and reviews repairs is doing comparable work, but API decides whether it qualifies. Describe the equipment, the codes your mill follows and your own role precisely on the application.

faq.q: Is the Tacoma LNG storage tank an API 510 vessel?
faq.a: Usually not. Large refrigerated LNG storage tanks are generally designed to low-pressure tank standards such as API 620 and API 625 rather than to ASME Section VIII, so API 510 does not normally govern the tank. The exchangers, separators and receivers in a liquefaction plant are a different matter: those are pressure vessels, and an owner may inspect them under API 510. Check the nameplate and design basis before you list the work on an API application.

faq.q: I have a process technology degree from Bellingham Technical College. Which eligibility route applies?
faq.a: If API accepts the degree as a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology, you need two years of experience in vessel design, construction, repair, operation or inspection, including at least one year supervising or performing inspection. If API treats it differently, the high school route of three years applies. Operating experience at a Whatcom or Skagit refinery can count, but only alongside real inspection work, so plan a move into the inspection group.

faq.q: Which pressure vessels does Washington exempt from state inspection?
faq.a: RCW 70.79.080 lists the exemptions. They include unfired vessels designed for no more than 15 psig, vessels of five cubic feet or less outside places of public assembly, vessels under 1.5 cubic feet or six inches in diameter anywhere, vessels under federal regulation and ambient-temperature water tanks with no air cushion. An exempt vessel may still sit inside an owner's API 510 programme; the exemption removes the state certificate, not the owner's duty to inspect.

faq.q: How long is the API 510 exam day for a Seattle candidate?
faq.a: The examination itself lasts about 7.5 hours: a short tutorial, 2.75 hours of closed-book questions, a 45-minute lunch break and 3.75 hours of open-book questions with the code PDFs on screen. Add the travel from the north Sound refineries or from Tacoma and it becomes a full day. Book a morning appointment and plan the night before so that the drive does not eat into your concentration.
